title: Pacing the Frontier, or Pacing the Narrative?
body:
On Saturday, Dario Amodei published an essay “We Must Pace the Frontier“ calling on AI companies to deliberately “slow the pace” at which they improve model capabilities. The framing, predictably, was existential: humanity needs time to catch up to the machines we’re building. Within hours, Sam Altman endorsed the idea on X and said OpenAI would adopt just* one* of the proposed safeguards. Elon Musk, whose Grok is nowhere near the frontier, also chimed in saying “Dario is right.”

I don’t buy this existential framing. Here’s an alternative hypothesis:

  • Model performance is plateauing, and Anthropic is arguably in second place now.
  • Compute and energy are getting dramatically more expensive, making larger models prohibitively expensive to train.
  • AI data centers are massively unpopular, and legislation looks increasingly likely if Democrats regain control of Congress in the midterms.
  • “Slowing down AI development” is a convenient excuse to explain slowing - progress, to justify reduced spending, and to buy back some public goodwill.

Bluntly, this looks more like an effort to save the IPO rather than humanity.

Why Now?

The timing is interesting. Fears over AI are at an all time high. This follows the publication of the high profile Hugging Face Incident, where a swarm of OpenAI agents broke out of their test environment and hacked into parts of an open-source cybersecurity platform. Amodei’s essay landed the same week an Anthropic researcher publicly resigned and set off a wave of online criticism. It followed directly on the heels of Anthropic’s own threat-intelligence report, which documented Claude being used for weapons development, cyber operations, surveillance, and fraud. Anthropic reported that suspected Houthi rebels attempted to use Claude to write guidance navigation and control programs to build guided missiles. This followed just days after they reported that they blocked attempts to use Claude to build biological weapons.

Somehow Anthropic made this meme a reality

These alarming headlines prompted US Senator Bernie Sanders [to demand a pause on advanced AI development](https://US Senator Bernie Sanders demanding a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence.) and a ban on artificial superintelligence (ASI). His bill includes criminal penalties including up to 20 years in federal prison for developers and the dissolution of companies (aka the “corporate death penalty”) that try to develop ASI. It would also create a new Cabinet-level federal agency, advised by outside AI experts, with authority to define what counts as “superintelligence,” set safety standards before a pause is lifted, and - per the bill’s own language - oversee the destruction of non-compliant systems. Sander’s bill is the Butlerian Jihad of AI legislation - by far the most aggressive anyone in Congress has proposed to date.

Aside from staying out of jail, the AI companies may have other reasons why they want to slow down development, first and foremost their own stagnating performance.

The Hype that hasn’t delivered

The hyperbolic claims of AI bros have proven hard for their models to live up to. Musk famously predicted the emergence of superintelligent AI in 2025 (he also predicted a Mars Base in 2024). Altman predicted that AI agents would “materially change the output of companies” in 2025. In contrast MIT’s Project NANDA found that 95% of enterprise generative AI pilots deliver no measurable financial impact. In his 2024 essay “Machines of Loving Grace” Dario predicted that beginning in 2026 AI would “double of the human lifespan to roughly 150.” Despite the obvious mathematical impossibility of Dario’s claim, AI has failed to deliver a single medical breakthrough.

Hyperbolic claims of super-intelligence and curing cancer aside, the performance of models on standardized benchmarks have improved... but the improvement appears to be plateauing.

Frontline model performance on MMLU benchmark. It only took 5 prompt for Claude to make this figure.

More importantly, despite AI models achieving higher benchmark scores, the promises of reducing headcount and increasing productivity have remained elusive. Robert Half found that 29% of companies that laid off staff for AI have already rehired for the exact same positions, and Forrester’s 2026 “Future of Work” report found 55% of employers who cut jobs for AI now call it the wrong decision.

Anthropic’s Position appears weaker now

Meanwhile, Anthropic’s position which was so dominant just a few months ago appears to be weakening. Qwen3.8-Max-0902 took #1 overall on Arena’s Code Arena: WebDev leaderboard in September, three points above Claude Opus 5, marking the first time this year an Anthropic model has been displaced at the top of a vote-based coding board. On Twitter and Reddit at least, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra model appears to be consuming most of the tech-bro oxygen, having seemingly eclipsed Claude’s Fable 5.1 for attention.

The Math doesn’t math at AI companies

AI profits may be stagnating as well. Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI has * ever* closed a year in the black.

Anthropic’s internal documents reportedly project a $14 billion loss for 2026, despite revenue rocketing from roughly $1 billion annualized in December 2024 to about $30 billion by April 2026. OpenAI’s numbers are even worse:

it’s burning roughly $17 billion in cash this year, doesn’t project positive free cash flow until 2029 at the earliest.

AI companies face soaring operating costs because AI data centers are creating severe global shortages in memory chips, graphics processing units (GPUs), and electricity. Gartner forecasts $2.59 trillion in worldwide AI spending for 2026, up 47% year over year, with infrastructure making up more than 45% of that total. The global shortage of high bandwidth memory has driven the manufacturers stocks to new highs, but has also driven up the cost of RAM. DDR5 chip prices went from $6.84 per GB in September 2025 to $27.20 per GB by December 2025, nearly a 300% jump in a single quarter. Meanwhile, US electricity prices have rates have risen over 40% since 2021. The combination of AI data center construction and the closure of the straight of Hormuz have further spiked global energy prices, resulting in a increasing of about 5.0% over the past year to roughly 18 cents per kilowatt-hour (kWh) as of mid-2026, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Nobody outside of the industry likes them

Outside of an insular group of tech bros and investors, AI is also becoming historically unpopular. According to a 2025 Pew Research survey only 10% of American’s are “more excited than concerned” about AI. Polls from 2026 by Gallup and Heatmap show that 71-75% of American’s are opposed to building more AI data centers and 77% of respondents in a Reuters poll worry that AI data centers will drive up local electricity costs. Despite a highly partisan electorate, American’s are in apparent agreement about AI, and it’s about as popular as the recent explosive diarrhea outbreak.

What’s wrong with Dario’s fix

First, it doesn’t propose anything that costs Anthropic a release. Amodei was explicit that pacing “does not mean halting model training or technical progress.” There’s no compute cap, no minimum evaluation period before a model ships, no metric anyone outside the company could use to check whether “pacing” happened on any given release. A commitment with no enforcement mechanism and no observable failure condition isn’t a policy - it’s a statement of intent, and statements of intent tend not to be honored when they become inconvenient.

Second, it keeps all of the actual power inside the companies it’s supposed to constrain. The third-party evaluators Amodei describes get access because Anthropic chooses to grant it. They get access to whatever systems and data Anthropic chooses to expose and their findings get acted on only if Anthropic chooses to act on them. Unlike a government regulator with statutory authority and subpoena power, the “third party evaluators” Dario envisions are essentially empowered to write a strongly worded email.

Third, the phrase “coordination among leading AI companies” is doing a lot of work while committing to nothing. Voluntary coordination between competitors on how fast to develop a commercial product is exactly the kind of behavior that antitrust law exists to scrutinize. This is probably why OpenAI reportedly sought legal guidance on whether a coordinated slowdown is even something rival labs can lawfully agree to. Depending on an illegal collusion between rivals doesn’t sound like a plan likely to succeed.

Fourth, and most tellingly: the proposal has no provision for what happens if a company decides pacing isn’t worth the competitive cost and stops. There’s no penalty or disclosure requirement. Compare that to Sanders’s bill, which has a mechanism for enforcement body and real penalties, however extreme they may be.

What we should do instead

Dario’s essay may be equal parts “dog ate my homework” excuse for lagging model performance/delayed IPO and legitimate concerns about AI safety. But we ought to take the second part seriously. We * should* be worried about AI safety, particularly the threat that

- not future - models could be used to develop biological weapons and aide in cyber attacks. But the solution isn’t to buy into Dario’s self-serving essay about future AI development. Instead of letting companies “pace” themselves, we ought to consider how they can be

Commercial flights have become significantly safer in recent decades | Our World in Data

current****regulated.

Creating agencies to define and enforce rules and to investigate safety lapses is essential. The FAA and NTSB split these responsibilities and have made air travel vastly safer over recent decades. This doesn’t mean “pausing” progress. Despite having the most stringent air safety regulations the US and Europe lead the world in aviation, despite China’s laxer regulation willingness to cut corners.

One lesson that we’ve learned from aviation - and recently relearned from Boeing’s 737 Max fiasco - is that industries should not be trusted to regulate themselves, especially when the stakes are high. We shouldn’t let these companies off the hook for real regulation, and we shouldn’t let them use Dario’s essay as an excuse to delay it.
